title: A heat wave hits. What does a cone cost?
hook: Everyone wants more ice cream. Does only the price move?

knows: that the market price sits where buyers' and sellers' lines cross
how a supply shift moves the crossing (flour-shock)
doesNotKnow: that a rise in demand moves price and quantity up together, along the sellers' line

misconception: A demand rise only changes the price.
objective: The learner can explain that when buyers want more at every price, sellers supply more only at a higher price, so price and quantity both rise: +30 cones of demand moves the crossing from $6 and 40 to $7.50 and 55.

claims.text: In the ice cream model (buyers want 100 − 10p, sellers supply 10p − 20) the lines cross at $6 and 40 cones.
If buyers want 30 more at every price, the lines cross at $7.50 and 55 cones.
At $9 sellers would bring 70 cones but buyers (wanting 130 − 10p) would want only 40, so cones would be left over and the price would fall back.
claims.source: 10 × 9 − 20 = 70; 130 − 90 = 40. The standard adjustment story for excess supply (e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 4).

claims.text: Other settings of the slider use the same algebra: price = (120 + extra) / 20, e.g. +15 → $6.75, +45 → $8.25, +60 → $9.
claims.source: eqPrice(x) = (120 + x) / 20. Shown in the reveal only for values the learner visited.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: straight lines, one market, invented numbers; real shifts are messier.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Toy ice cream market: straight lines'.

recall.question: A new festival makes more people want hotel rooms at every price. In a simple supply-and-demand model, what happens?
options: Price rises; the number of rooms rented stays the same
Price and rooms rented both rise
Rooms rented rise; price stays the same
recall.why: The demand line shifts out, and the crossing moves up along the supply line: sellers offer more rooms only at a higher price, so both rise.
